title: Treasury Cash Ladder & Liquidity Constraints
question: Which cash can wait until maturity?
audience: Treasury, corporate-finance and risk analysts challenging whether an investment allocation can meet a dated payment schedule.
data: Official U.S. Treasury daily bill quotations for 2025 and 2026, retrieved October 30, 2026. Latest observation: October 29. Use 4-, 8- and 13-week bank discount quotes. Capital, payments, reserve and proportional fees are hypothetical.
methods: Linear programming with explicit capital, payment-date and minimum-cash constraints. Convert bank discount quotes to modeled purchase-to-maturity factors. An independent JavaScript vertex solver checks the Python HiGHS solution. SQL audits capital and the minimum reserve. Test early stress payments, reserve levels and fees.
findings: The reference $1 million scenario earns $6,279 above zero-yield cash after $700,000 of modeled payments, while preserving at least $100,000 of spendable cash at each tested date. It holds $150,000 uninvested so the day-14 stress payment can clear. The result uses indicative October 29 quotes and assumed maturities; it is not an executed return.
implications: A headline yield is insufficient when money is needed before maturity. Use a dated cash forecast to limit what can be invested, then test reserve and fee assumptions before seeking executable prices.
limitations: Fixed 28-, 56- and 91-day tenors approximate security dates. No early sale, reinvestment, taxes, lot sizes, bid-ask spread or holiday adjustment is modeled. Treasury bid quotations are not executable offers. The baseline cash yield is assumed zero. No real company cash flow or achieved investment return is claimed.
summary: A $1 million cash scenario earns a modeled $6,279 while meeting every payment and reserve constraint. The allocation is driven by when cash is needed, as well as the quoted yield.

evidence.caption: Hypothetical cash after each modeled payment, using observed October 29 Treasury quotations. The dashed line is the assumed $100,000 reserve, not an observed company requirement.

title: Workforce Replacement & Recruiting Capacity
question: How much hiring does growth really require?
audience: Workforce-planning, operations, research and consulting analysts assessing whether recruiting capacity and hiring budgets can support a headcount target.
data: Official BLS JOLTS monthly seasonally adjusted levels and rates for seven national industry aggregates, January 2015 through August 2026. Latest month is preliminary. Separate release-table values audit three months. Employer staffing, growth, cost and hiring capacity are hypothetical.
methods: Analytical headcount recurrence separates replacement hires from net expansion. Use a trailing 12-month mean separation rate as a clearly labeled industry proxy. Independently reconcile inputs in SQL and 126 source-table cells. Chronologically select among four prespecified forecasting baselines using 2023-2024 validation and evaluate 2025-2026 held-out target windows.
findings: At the 3.56% trailing mean monthly private-sector separation rate, a hypothetical employer growing from 1,000 to 1,100 staff needs about 548 hires over twelve months. Roughly 448 replace exits. Forecast methods selected on validation beat the last-month baseline in four of seven series, tie in one and do worse in two. This does not establish production forecast quality.
implications: A budget for 100 new roles may leave most recruiting work unaccounted for. Test replacement demand and monthly hiring capacity together, then replace the industry proxy with company-level exit evidence before approving a plan.
limitations: National rates are not employer-level exit probabilities. The model applies the proxy to beginning-month staff, which differs from the official denominator. Targets, costs and capacity are scenarios. Revised and concurrently adjusted data prevent a real-time backtest claim. Target windows and industry aggregates overlap. No causal conclusion, predictive interval or actual employer result is claimed.
summary: 100 net new roles can require about 548 hires in the reference scenario. Replacement demand changes the recruiting budget and can expose a capacity shortfall.

evidence.caption: Hypothetical 1,000-to-1,100 staffing plans calibrated to observed industry separation rates. Replacement hires and the assumed 100-person net increase are shown separately.

title: Private Credit Measurement & Funding Exposure
question: Who funds private credit, and which totals are comparable?
audience: Credit, investment research and financial-risk analysts deciding where more funding and valuation diligence is needed.
data: Official Federal Reserve October 16, 2026 publication, with rounded balance sheets observed at 2025 Q4. Public aggregate tables only; confidential Form PF microdata are not used. Hypothetical marks and an equity/assets screen are separate from observed balances.
methods: Source-table extraction, units and scope reconciliation, independent SQL equity identities, and accounting mark-down scenarios on U.S. private loans and corporate equities. Reverse-solve the mark that reaches an assumed equity/assets screen. Preserve source blanks and rounding residuals; exclude CLOs from equity comparisons.
findings: The publication reports $1.458 trillion of private loans to U.S. businesses, while the nonfinancial-business debt table reports $1.310 trillion, or 5.62% of that debt denominator. The difference is scope. Bank funding of credit vehicles is a separate intermediation layer. Newly identifying the sector in 2026 does not mean its existing balances were newly borrowed.
implications: Reconcile borrower and vehicle scope before comparing exposure totals or adding intermediation layers. Use the scenario explorer to identify what further funding, valuation and instrument-detail evidence would be needed before judging a vehicle type.
limitations: The observations are 2025 Q4, not live 2026 holdings. Aggregate fund populations hide dispersion. CLO equity is not separately reported and is not treated as zero. Missing maturity, withdrawal and unencumbered-cash data prevent a redemption or liquidity model. No default probability, regulatory solvency finding or institution-level contagion is established.
summary: A 2026 measurement change makes private credit more visible. A scope ledger separates $1.458 trillion of broad business lending from $1.310 trillion in the nonfinancial-business debt table.

evidence.caption: Observed rounded 2025 Q4 balances from an October 2026 Federal Reserve publication. CLOs are excluded here because equity is not separately reported.

title: Import Duties & Sourcing Tradeoffs
question: Did import-duty exposure change, or did the sourcing basket change?
audience: Procurement, commercial-finance and consulting analysts identifying product groups that warrant quote, classification and sourcing diligence.
data: Official Census August 2025 and August 2026 detailed import archives. Primary comparison: January-August YTD imports for consumption and calculated duties. Prespecified HS4 groups 8504, 8507 and 8541. Scenario budgets and switching costs are hypothetical.
methods: Fixed-width extraction and exact reconciliation to independently published commodity totals. Positive-value, identical-description HTS10/origin panels separate starting-basket rate changes from composition. Report matched value coverage and August-only sensitivity. Sourcing pairs standardize both origins to a common source basket with at least 80% coverage; SQL independently reconciles totals.
findings: Full-population historical duty ratios rise from 8.57% to 12.61% for transformers/converters/inductors and from 14.11% to 16.97% for accumulators; semiconductor-device ratios move from 7.23% to 7.27%. Only 46.7% of 2026 accumulator value enters the strict cross-year panel, so its decomposition cannot be generalized to the whole category.
implications: Inspect product comparability and coverage before treating an origin-level average as a sourcing opportunity. The tool tests which hypothetical supplier premium and switching cost would offset a historical duty difference; it does not select a supplier or quote a legal tariff.
limitations: Calculated duties are not final collections or causal tariff incidence. Same-code cells can conceal quality and supplier changes. Countries are not suppliers. Current legal rates, origin eligibility, quotes, capacity, freight and switching feasibility are not established. Historical retrieved files may contain revisions, and modeled budget differences are not observed savings.
summary: Import-duty ratios and sourcing mix can move in different directions. A strict comparison exposes a major coverage gap before turning historical duty differences into a budget scenario.

evidence.caption: Actual Census value retained by the strict HTS10/origin match. The 2026 accumulator and semiconductor panels have materially incomplete coverage.

title: Fuel Retail Investment Decision Lab
question: Can the sales estimate support the development budget?
audience: Investment, lending, finance and consulting analysts testing a development case before capital is committed.
data: Anonymized numerical extracts from two user-supplied April 2026 feasibility and risk documents. Sales are unverified report estimates. Costs, margins, staffing, financing, wash economics and ramp inputs are explicitly hypothetical. Official Texas references support the commission minimum and general due-diligence checks.
methods: Reconcile reported sales, separate lottery ticket proceeds from commission, calculate contribution and pre-tax cash available for debt, amortize a hypothetical loan, and model sponsor-funded fees, draw-based interest, carry and an opening ramp. Compare 24 scope/sales/delay cases, reverse-solve coverage thresholds and audit 31 ordinal risk records. SQL independently reconciles contribution, and Python and JavaScript agree across 33 scenarios.
findings: The report’s average $138,031 monthly nonfuel receipts reconcile. Under the reference hypothetical economics, cash available for debt is $16,504 against a $16,888 payment: 0.98x stabilized coverage. The sales ramp lowers opening-year coverage to 0.61x, below the chosen 1.25x screen. Four of 31 risk labels conflict with the source’s own rules.
implications: Replace broad claims of feasibility with explicit financing conditions and evidence gates. Change costs, margins, sales and loan inputs to see what would restore coverage. A passing scenario still leaves civil site fit, access, environmental condition and other project-specific approvals unresolved.
limitations: No actual budget, lender quote, operating history or underlying market study was supplied. Sales categories may overlap and require clarification. Financing capacity is not fair value. Taxes, terminal value, refinancing and future working-capital changes are excluded. The model claims no actual return, savings, business impact or event probabilities. Original reports and identifying details are not distributed.
summary: The sales totals reconcile. In one explicit cost and financing illustration, debt coverage is 0.98x. An underwriting lab shows what would have to change and which evidence is still missing.

evidence.caption: Report estimates plus hypothetical economics. Lottery ticket proceeds are separated from retailer commission; contribution includes net fuel income. These are not actual operating results.

title: Real Wages & Payroll Budget Tradeoffs
question: When does a pay rise buy more?
audience: Economic researchers and workforce-finance teams separating purchasing power from nominal pay growth.
data: 237 monthly rows from January 2007 through September 2026. BLS hourly earnings, weekly hours and CPI-U are seasonally adjusted. October 2025 CPI is missing and remains unfilled, leaving 236 real-pay observations.
methods: Calendar-aligned earnings and CPI, exact log decomposition, twelve-month changes without forward filling, three prespecified comparison anchors and an independent SQL reconciliation. A separate calculator solves a hypothetical real weekly pay target.
findings: Real hourly earnings rose 2.1% from February 2020 to September 2026; real weekly earnings rose 2.4%. Over the latest twelve months, real hourly earnings fell 0.7% and real weekly earnings fell 0.1%. The conclusion depends on the comparison period.
implications: Separate hourly pay, hours and inflation before choosing a payroll assumption. The workbench makes the inflation rate, hours change and real-pay target explicit; it does not recommend a compensation rate.
limitations: National averages change with the mix of workers and industries. They do not measure the same people over time or describe Houston wages. CPI-U is not an individual household budget. Benefits, employer payroll taxes and irregular bonuses are excluded. Revised history is not a real-time forecast, and missing CPI collection affects adjacent estimates.
summary: Real hourly earnings rose 2.1% from February 2020, but fell 0.7% in the latest twelve months. Hours and inflation explain why the comparison period matters.

evidence.caption: Observed BLS series through September 2026, rebased to February 2020 = 100. Real pay divides earnings by CPI-U. The October 2025 CPI gap remains missing.

title: Diesel Fuel Budget Risk: A 13-Week Reserve Test
question: How much diesel-price risk should a budget carry?
audience: Operations, procurement and FP&A teams reviewing cash reserves for a thirteen-week fuel budget.
data: 1,035 weekly EIA U.S. retail diesel observations through October 26, 2026, including taxes. Historical prices are observed. The 100,000-gallon quarterly exposure and equal weekly purchases are hypothetical.
methods: 79 complete non-overlapping thirteen-week blocks. Each rule uses a prior-week quote and completed historical targets. A 2016 to 2019 validation period selects the reserve window before a 2020 onward holdout. SQL independently verifies realized quarter means and shortfalls.
findings: The historical q90 reserve covered 20 of 26 holdout quarters (76.9%), compared with 24 of 26 (92.3%) for a fixed 10% buffer. Its average reserve was 7.2% above the quote. The worst shortfall was $22,176 at an assumed 100,000 gallons. The historical rule missed its nominal coverage target.
implications: Compare protection against budget capacity tied up in reserve. A simpler, larger buffer covered more historical quarters. Use the workbench to inspect price and volume assumptions before applying the idea to actual fleet invoices.
limitations: Retail national prices differ from local fleet contracts and wholesale hedges. Fuel specifications changed over the historical series. There are only 26 holdout quarters, and serial dependence remains possible. Current revised history is not a point-in-time vintage backtest. Historical coverage is not a future probability guarantee. Unused reserve is not savings.
summary: A historical reserve covered 20 of 26 quarters. A fixed 10% buffer covered 24. The comparison makes the cost of a smaller reserve visible.

evidence.caption: Actual EIA prices compared with three budget rules in completed holdout quarters. Budgets use a prior-week quote; realized prices are thirteen-week means.

title: Catalyst Pricing & Contract Economics
question: What changed the margin, and which contracts need review?
audience: Commercial finance and pricing teams reviewing customer and product profitability.
data: 180 synthetic customer-product-period records across 30 fictional customers and two illustrative annual snapshots. No company operating data are used.
methods: Python and SQL separate volume, product/customer mix, realized price and variable cost in an exactly reconciling ordered margin bridge. A 135-case grid varies price, elasticity, churn and cost inflation.
findings: In the simulation, variable contribution falls by $157,706. Higher realized prices add $979,360, while higher unit costs subtract $1,380,513. Volume and mix complete the reconciliation. Revenue growth alone would miss the cost pressure.
implications: Use the bridge to identify contracts for review before proposing a general price increase. Check service-cost allocations and test how demand could respond.
limitations: Elasticities, churn and allocated service costs are invented. The three-year NPV excludes tax, capex, working capital and service costs. No willingness to pay or actual savings is estimated.
summary: Higher prices did not offset rising costs in this simulated customer portfolio. A margin bridge explains the $157,706 decline in contribution.

title: Credit Card Acquisition Economics
question: Does a higher conversion rate create more value?
audience: Consumer-finance acquisition and campaign teams deciding whether to scale an incentive.
data: A fully synthetic randomized campaign with 12,000 fictional prospects and assumed account economics.
methods: Intention-to-treat conversion comparison, segment standardization, a three-year account NPV model and a conversion-only parametric bootstrap. Eighty-one scenarios vary credit loss, funding and retention.
findings: Treatment conversion is 0.89 percentage points higher in the simulation, but modeled incremental NPV is negative at $2.20 per prospect. Neither uncertainty interval rules out zero: the lift interval is −0.19 to 1.96 points, and the conditional NPV interval is −$10.80 to $5.34.
implications: The simulated result does not support scaling the incentive. Evaluate acquisition costs, losses and retention alongside conversion, then collect stronger evidence of value.
limitations: All prospects and parameters are simulated. Uncertainty covers conversion conditional on the assumed economics, not full business uncertainty. This is not a lending engine or an observed customer result.
summary: A simulated incentive increased conversion, but its estimated value per prospect fell. The case separates acquisition growth from risk-adjusted economics.

title: Grid Resilience Capital Allocation
question: Which upgrades deserve a limited investment budget?
audience: An investment committee balancing outage-related social value, crew capacity and critical-service commitments.
data: EIA 2023/2024 state reliability benchmarks for ten selected states, combined with fictional districts, projects and investment assumptions.
methods: An exact finite-scenario optimizer evaluates 59,049 allocations under budget, crew and service constraints. Equal-weight optimization, a greedy baseline, an independent dynamic-programming check and coverage sensitivity challenge the choice.
findings: The model selects three upgrades and reserves $7.716 million of a $20 million envelope. Its worst specified social NPV is $0.827 million, compared with −$8.539 million for the comparison plans. An additional stress outside the original scenario set produces −$6.316 million.
implications: The case makes the cost of different allocation rules visible. It supports questions for engineering and investment review, with no guarantee that the chosen scenarios cover future conditions.
limitations: Project costs, effectiveness and outage valuation are hypothetical. The objective is social value, not utility cash profit. State averages are not feeder forecasts, and robustness applies only to the specified uncertainty set.
summary: A constrained investment model selects three hypothetical upgrades. It also shows why a plan that survives the chosen scenarios can still fail a harsher stress.

title: Outpatient Access & Capacity Simulation
question: What does better appointment access cost?
audience: Outpatient scheduling and operations leaders reviewing urgent and routine booking policies.
data: Synthetic requests, administrative urgency labels, no-show probabilities and staffing assumptions. No patient data or clinical predictions are used.
methods: Paired booking simulations use common random streams, ten development replications for policy selection and thirty separate holdout replications. Capacity audits, unbooked requests and arrival/absence stresses retain operational constraints.
findings: Across thirty holdout simulations, the selected policy books all urgent requests within one business day and all routine requests within seven. Under the assumed visit and staffing costs, incremental contribution versus first-come-first-served is −$53,600.
implications: Review urgent and routine access together with staffing, attendance and unbooked demand. A shorter average wait does not establish that a policy is affordable or ready for clinical use.
limitations: The results are conditional simulation outcomes, not clinical effectiveness or observed revenue. Assumed advance knowledge of capacity lost to absence is optimistic. Continuity, patient preferences and real staffing distributions need prospective validation.
summary: The simulated scheduling policy meets both booking targets, but reduces modeled contribution. Better access comes with a staffing tradeoff.

title: Mobility Demand Forecasting & Capacity Economics
question: Does a better rental forecast improve a capacity plan?
audience: An operations planner deciding how a rental forecast should influence a capacity rule.
data: 731 daily observations from the UCI Bike Sharing dataset, covering historical 2011–2012 Capital Bikeshare rentals. Capacity-cost inputs are hypothetical.
methods: Five forecast specifications, chronological validation, rolling one-day-ahead predictions and a separate 184-day test period. Validation selects ridge regression with penalty 1. Residuals inform asymmetric-cost planning rules.
findings: On 184 test days, the selected ridge model has weighted absolute percentage error of 13.35%, compared with 18.70% for a seven-day seasonal baseline. Its nominal 90% prediction band covers 87.5% of observations, below the intended level.
implications: Compare forecasting methods using both error and the consequences of underplanning or overplanning. The capacity-cost examples depend on assumed costs and do not measure operational savings.
limitations: The target is realized rentals, not uncensored demand. Trip-equivalent capacity is not a physical fleet-size recommendation. Any modeled cost difference is a counterfactual under invented costs, not observed savings.
summary: The selected model reduces historical test error from 18.70% to 13.35%. A separate planning model tests what those errors could cost.

title: Utility Reliability Due Diligence Lab
question: Can we trust the latest reliability data?
audience: An analyst reviewing utility peers and deciding which source releases can inform due diligence.
data: Six official EIA reliability workbooks from 2020–2025: 11,552 method-specific records across 1,010 utility-state keys, with original workbook, sheet and row lineage.
methods: Python ETL, SQLite aggregation, method-consistent peer cohorts, state-total reconciliation and report-year-separated model testing. Utility-cluster bootstrap uncertainty checks whether an apparent accuracy gain is convincing.
findings: All 51 available state summaries reconcile in each of 2023 and 2024. Twenty-six summaries in 2025 exceed the 0.11-minute reconciliation tolerance. The workbench uses 2024 and retains the newer discrepancies for investigation. A separate predictive candidate also fails its approval checks.
implications: Check a release before treating it as an upgrade. Analysts can inspect comparable utility groups using the reconciled year while pursuing the unresolved source differences.
limitations: The predictive candidate also fails promotion: its improvement interval crosses zero and nominal interval coverage falls short. That diagnostic uses the quarantined source year. No engineering recommendation or actual upgrade saving is established.
summary: Twenty-six state summaries fail reconciliation in the 2025 release. The workbench keeps that release out of its decision inputs.

title: Airline Delay Intervention Screen
question: Where should a delay investigation start?
audience: An airline operations team with ten investigation slots and a limit of two sites per airport.
data: 60,093 official BTS carrier-airport-month source rows from January 2024 to August 2026. The pipeline quarantines 148 rows and retains 35,270 peer-eligible monthly rows.
methods: Leave-one-out airport/month benchmarking separates unusual carrier delay from raw size. Discovery priorities are frozen on January–August 2024, checked in 2025 and diagnosed in 2026. Two-month blocks examine retrospective stability.
findings: The frozen shortlist captures 43.38% of eligible positive peer excess in the 2026 diagnostic period, compared with 33.34% for the raw-burden baseline. The 10.04-point difference measures how the shortlist concentrates an accounting benchmark. It is not a reduction in delay minutes.
implications: Use the shortlist to request operational evidence at the selected carrier-airport sites. Comparable schedules, aircraft, staffing and maintenance data are needed before proposing and evaluating a pilot.
limitations: The data omit flight-level schedule, fleet and route comparability, and use a revised snapshot. No causal intervention effect, attainable saving or point-in-time backtest is established.
summary: A fixed shortlist captures more eligible peer-excess delay than a raw-burden ranking. It prioritizes investigation rather than claiming an intervention effect.

title: Bank Deposit Cost Attribution
question: Why did bank deposit interest expense fall?
audience: Bank treasury and finance teams reviewing balance growth, interest-bearing mix and pricing pressure.
data: A pinned FDIC panel of 48,814 bank-quarters across eleven dates. The matched screen retains 4,018 banks and 91% of latest domestic deposits.
methods: Quarterly/YTD reconciliation and deposit-stock checks precede an exact three-factor Shapley attribution. Six replacement orders allocate interactions symmetrically. Cohort screens and hypothetical attrition scenarios test sensitivity.
findings: From Q2 2025 to Q2 2026, quarterly domestic deposit interest expense falls by $5.012 billion in the screened cohort. Balance growth adds $5.242 billion, interest-bearing mix adds $0.057 billion and the proxy-rate component subtracts $10.310 billion. The contributions reconcile to the total.
implications: Use the breakdown to frame a treasury pricing review. Account-level rates, renewal dates and customer behavior are needed before assuming a rate cut will save money after attrition and replacement funding.
limitations: The proxy rate is derived from endpoint-average balances and absorbs composition and timing effects. It is not a quoted product rate or causal deposit beta. Certificate matching and a growth screen do not fully remove acquisition effects.
summary: Quarterly deposit interest expense falls by $5.01 billion across 4,018 screened banks. The bridge separates balances, mix and a derived rate measure.

title: Insurance Reserve Challenge Lab
question: How sensitive is a reserve estimate to the tail?
audience: A finance and actuarial diligence committee deciding where further reserve investigation is needed.
data: 4,046 paid/incurred cells from six original 2025 insurer filings. Thirty-one of forty-eight disclosed triangles meet the selected development gates.
methods: Gated paid-development chain ladder, volume and median methods, masked-diagonal benchmark comparisons and explicit tail sensitivities. Source scope and numerical cells are retained.
findings: The development method has 14.54% weighted absolute percentage error across 468 masked one-step cells, compared with 44.50% for repeating the latest increment. Adding a 1.10 tail factor raises the modeled unpaid balance by $17.12 billion. The result shows substantial sensitivity to late claims development.
implications: Investigate the largest tail sensitivities first. Request actuarial selections, claims-handling changes and reinsurance detail before discussing reserves or capital returns.
limitations: The current disclosure contains revised historical cells, so this is not an as-released forecast. Older claims, expense scope and sparse late-development factors matter. The model does not justify reserve release or capital returns.
summary: A modest change to the assumed claims-development tail adds $17.12 billion to the modeled unpaid balance. The gap warrants investigation, not a reserve release.

title: Retail REIT Refinancing Resilience
question: When does rolling over debt stop being enough?
audience: A treasury and finance committee reviewing a five-year refinancing plan against cash floors.
data: Six original 2025 REIT filings disclose $53.25 billion of face principal, including $31.23 billion due in 2026–2030. Entity scope, cash facts and historical operating cash flows are reconciled.
methods: Five-year cash paths produce exact affine constraints on a common rollover fraction. Independent linear programming checks the bounds. Persistent CFO shocks, spread changes and recovery cases challenge feasibility.
findings: All six issuers pass the unchanged-CFO, full-rollover baseline. Thirty-seven of ninety issuer/scenario combinations cannot meet all five cash floors using rollover alone. No issuer remains feasible across the expanded scenario grid. These are conditional stresses with no assigned probabilities.
implications: Use the cash-floor frontier to identify questions about funding flexibility. Validate committed facilities, extensions, recurring property investment and distribution requirements before drawing a current liquidity conclusion.
limitations: This is a dated annual-base scenario, not current liquidity or a refinancing approval. Cash floors, capex, fees and spreads are assumptions; shocks have no assigned probabilities. Market access and actual covenants require further diligence.
summary: Thirty-seven of ninety financing scenarios fail the assumed cash floors even with full debt rollover. The model exposes the conditions behind that result.

title: Inventory Funding & Forecast Governance
question: Should a more complex inventory forecast replace the baseline?
audience: Procurement and treasury analysts deciding which inventory balance forecast can support further planning.
data: 332 coherent SEC company-quarters and 1,160 retained source figures, with 47 later test outcomes across five semiconductor-equipment issuers.
methods: Filing-availability-aware rolling ridge estimates use separate selection, calibration and test windows. Last-balance and seasonal baselines, issuer-cluster uncertainty and source-definition exclusions check model and data risk.
findings: Across 47 later outcomes, candidate WAPE is 3.025%, versus 2.624% for the last balance. The nominal 90% bands cover 86.11% of 36 eligible outcomes. The candidate is not approved for use. Only four issuers have consistently defined current inputs for the planning screen.
implications: Keep the baseline and repair source-definition gaps before testing a new model. Procurement planning also requires inventory aging, purchase commitments and service constraints.
limitations: Only four issuers have coherent current inputs. Five dependent sector histories limit uncertainty assessment. Inventory balance is not a procurement cash forecast, and assumed carry-cost examples are not savings.
summary: The ridge model performs worse than the last disclosed inventory balance. The simpler baseline remains the default.

title: Reinvestment & Cash Return Review
question: How do cash returns sit alongside reinvestment?
audience: Corporate finance and treasury teams reviewing distributions against capital commitments.
data: 32 admitted company-years and 256 SEC source figures. Latest comparisons use a coherent FY2025 across Union Pacific, CSX and Norfolk Southern.
methods: Original-filing reconciliation, a cash-return subtotal, reverse CFO stress and three-year coverage. Net/gross productive-asset and tax/hurdle sensitivity expose the limits of accounting-return proxies.
findings: Across Union Pacific, CSX and Norfolk Southern in FY2025, operating cash totals $18.264 billion, cash PP&E capex $8.897 billion, and dividends plus repurchases $10.032 billion. The specified residual is −$665 million, with two issuers showing a negative subtotal.
implications: Review distributions alongside maintenance, safety and committed growth spending. Other cash sources and uses belong in the actual treasury plan before changing investment or shareholder returns.
limitations: Cash is fungible: this subtotal does not show which payment was debt-funded or establish a current funding deficit. Fixed-asset proxies are not issuer ROIC. Safe capex cuts cannot be inferred from the scenario controls.
summary: Three railroads distribute more than FY2025 operating cash less reported cash capex. The $665 million subtotal is a prompt for treasury review, not proof of a funding deficit.

title: Homebuilder Land Option Diligence
question: When might walking away from a land contract be rational?
audience: Homebuilder acquisition and finance teams reviewing deposits, optional future outlays and contract boundaries.
data: 74 contract-scope/date records from 24 original SEC numerical filing snapshots. Disclosed capital-at-risk bases and observation dates differ by issuer.
methods: A source-linked contract register reconciles total and component scopes. Two-stage exercise, wait and abandon choices are evaluated in 243 assumed scenarios and 27 refund sensitivities.
findings: The retained disclosures reconcile $1.613 billion of mixed-basis capital at risk and $13.711 billion of conditional remaining purchase prices. Contract scopes and dates differ. The exercise, wait and abandon scenarios use hypothetical values and terms rather than estimated parcel option values.
implications: Request tract-level values, refund rights, extension terms and minimum purchase schedules. A sunk deposit is relevant exposure, but does not by itself make a future purchase attractive.
limitations: Parcel values, probabilities, discounts, extension costs and refundability are assumed. The scenarios are not estimated option values or company-specific acquisition recommendations. A reused accounting tag does not establish a legal refund right.
summary: A contract register separates deposits already at risk from conditional future purchases. The option scenarios show why those are different decisions.

title: Hotel Reimbursement Economics
question: How does reimbursement accounting change a hotel margin comparison?
audience: Hotel-management/franchising FP&A and program-budget committees comparing operating performance.
data: 34 issuer-period observations, including 22 annual periods, from 12 original SEC filings for Marriott, Hilton and Choice Hotels. Exact original-source figures and matched periods are retained.
methods: Reported-income identities and matched year-over-year bridges isolate reimbursement revenue and costs. A 216-case scenario grid tests incremental program spending against explicit income-floor assumptions.
findings: Across the selected operators in H1 2026, reported revenue totals $20.784 billion, including $13.926 billion in reimbursements. The net reimbursement balance is −$326 million. Excluding reimbursement revenue and net balances changes the margin ordering of two issuers, without isolating pure fee profitability.
implications: Reconcile both income and revenue before comparing margins or approving program spending. Recoverability terms and a forward budget are needed to assess the cash and operating consequences.
limitations: The net balance is an accrual subtotal, not a current cash deficit. Normalization does not isolate pure fee profit or remove all mix differences. Budget scenarios hold the other business fixed and are not earnings forecasts.
summary: Reimbursements make up much of the selected operators’ reported revenue. Adjusting the denominator changes the apparent margin comparison.

title: Houston Mortgage Price Comparability
question: How comparable are Houston lenders’ mortgage prices?
audience: Consumer-finance researchers deciding which historical lender-price comparisons have observable common support.
data: 123,445 public Houston-area HMDA originated loans from the pinned 2025 vintage. Product and completeness checks retain 32,095 eligible observations.
methods: The five largest eligible lenders are selected by counts before inspecting prices. Coarsened matching uses public loan, leverage, debt-to-income and geography bands; 400 tract perturbations examine descriptive stability.
findings: The five selected lenders have 9,344 eligible loans. Of those, 3,867 fall in 18 borrower/loan groups represented at every lender, retaining 41.38%. The observed price-spread range changes from 2.001 to 1.902 percentage points after matching. The remaining gap is descriptive.
implications: Check which borrowers a comparison represents before ranking lender averages. For a borrower decision, request dated Loan Estimates for the same product and review rates, fees, credits and holding period.
limitations: Missing credit scores, incentives, channels and shopping behavior leave hidden selection. Remaining differences are descriptive, not lender effects or current offers. Workbench rates, fees and holding periods are hypothetical.
summary: Only 41.38% of eligible loans at the five selected lenders enter the common-support comparison. The analysis makes that restriction visible before comparing prices.

title: Upstream Retirement Obligation Review
question: Can a book retirement liability become a cash budget?
audience: Upstream corporate finance and acquisition diligence teams assessing retirement-reserve evidence.
data: 17 original SEC annual filings across six issuers; 35 reconciled issuer-year retirement-obligation ledgers reconstructed from 257 operands.
methods: Opening balances and movements are reconciled to original disclosures, separating cash evidence from settlements and transfers. Linear-programming bounds test conditional timing, discount and near-term-share constraints.
findings: The latest observed book retirement obligation totals $15.275 billion at December 31, 2025. Only six explicit cash-paid observations are identified, all for one issuer. Eighteen of 216 timing cases are infeasible under their assumed constraints, which does not imply issuer insolvency.
implications: Request asset-level retirement schedules, engineering cost estimates, discount layers and transfer agreements before approving a cash reserve. Separate payments from liability movements caused by dispositions or remeasurement.
limitations: A discounted book stock does not identify nominal cash or its timing. Exact mathematical bounds remain conditional on assumed rates and timing constraints. Infeasible assumptions do not imply issuer insolvency.
summary: The disclosures support a reconciled liability ledger, but do not identify the full cash payment schedule. Timing assumptions produce a range rather than a forecast.

title: Credit Spread Recession Signal Audit
question: Do credit spreads improve a recession model enough to use it?
audience: Credit-research model-governance reviewers assessing incremental predictive value.
data: Pinned monthly FRED spreads, Treasury yields and NBER recession labels: 648 panel origins, with 192 held-out origins from 2008–2023 and labels through 2024.
methods: Expanding logistic estimation uses prior-month features, a twelve-month label gap, training-only scaling and separate penalty selection. Curve and historical-probability baselines, paired blocks and SQL checks challenge the candidate.
findings: Across 192 held-out forecast dates, Brier loss is 0.1676 for credit plus curve, 0.1750 for the curve model and 0.1487 for the expanding historical baseline. Lower loss is better. The candidate therefore fails its simplest benchmark despite improving on the curve model.
implications: Preserve the failed comparison and withhold approval. Testing another design requires new evaluation evidence, rather than retuning the reviewed test until it looks positive.
limitations: The paired uncertainty band crosses zero and testing includes only two separate recession-target episodes. Revised data and eventual NBER labels do not recreate real-time knowledge. This is not a live recession forecast or a validated trading signal.
summary: Credit spreads improve one model comparison but lose to a simple historical probability. The candidate is not approved for use.

title: Restaurant Lease & Operating Leverage Review
question: When do fixed restaurant commitments exceed response capacity?
audience: Restaurant corporate finance and operations committees investigating an earnings stress.
data: 32 SEC company-years across six operators. Twenty-four latest source facts reconcile to six original filings; selected fiscal ends differ.
methods: Lease-aware earnings stress avoids deducting base rent already included in EBIT. A bounded two-lever response model is checked against independent linear programming across 216 cases, with 72 additional sensitivities.
findings: Selected FY2025 lease expense totals $1.089 billion, versus $1.099 billion in lease payments. Thirty-two of 216 reference cases cannot meet the assumed earnings floor within the response caps. Thirty-three are feasible only when both cost savings and sales recovery are available.
implications: Investigate store contribution margins, lease resets, execution costs and credible sales recovery before approving a response. Earnings sensitivity alone does not establish liquidity or covenant headroom.
limitations: Sales shocks, contribution margins, resource weights and response caps are assumptions. Earnings and lease cash are different concepts. The exercise establishes no actual savings, current liquidity gap or covenant result.
summary: Thirty-two assumed earnings stresses remain infeasible within the modeled response caps. The model also avoids deducting rent twice.

title: SEC Working Capital Optimization
question: Does releasing working capital create economic value?
audience: Corporate finance, treasury and procurement teams evaluating a working-capital diagnostic and limited pilot.
data: Fifteen publicly traded technology, device, semiconductor and infrastructure companies, using FY2025–FY2026 annual filings. A 150-fact ledger records selected SEC XBRL values, accessions, tags and reporting periods.
methods: Python and independent SQL calculations use average beginning/end balances and a 365-day convention for receivable, inventory and payable days. Cohort filters contextualize comparisons; a separate Apple scenario varies days, realization, implementation costs and financing rates.
findings: The Apple base scenario produces about $2.44 billion of one-time gross liquidity release. At an assumed 5% financing rate, that supports about $122 million of annual financing benefit, below the assumed $350 million first-year implementation cost. The fifteen-company comparison provides context, not attainable cash-cycle targets.
implications: Separate balance-sheet liquidity from profit and economic value. Investigate receivable quality, service levels, supplier terms and implementation costs before assessing a limited pilot or broader rollout.
limitations: The scenarios have no identified causal effect or demonstrated operational feasibility. Fiscal dates, classifications and business models differ; cohort medians remain descriptive, and Amazon is a single-member reference. The Streamlit application is externally hosted and may cold-start. The external server timed out during this portfolio release’s availability check.
summary: The illustrative Apple case releases cash, but its first-year financing benefit does not cover the assumed implementation cost.
